newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serbs vow to keep control of disputed town.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serbs vow to keep control of disputed town.

text.p: Bosnian Serb leaders warned on Thursday that war could reignite in the Balkans if the disputed town of Brcko were awarded to their Moslem-Croat rivals through international arbitration.
"I would like to say clearly here that Brcko is Serb and must remain Serb," Biljana Plavsic, president of Bosnia's Serb republic, said in a speech delivered in the northern town.
"I call on everyone to examine the problem realistically, warning that those who would like to play with the issue of Brcko are again invoking the spectre of war in this area."

Bosnian Serb authorities organised a ceremony marking the founding of their autonomous territory, the Serb republic, in Brcko town on Thursday to coincide with an arbitration hearing this week in Rome.
The first arbitration session to settle the status of Brcko opened on Wednesday, attended by delegations from Bosnia's Serb republic and Moslem-Croat federation.
No details of the arbitration have been released and reporters have been barred from the meeting site.
The Dayton peace agreement which ended the Bosnian war failed to resolve the fate of the strategic town which links Bosnian Serb territory to the west and east.
The narrow corridor that straddles the Sava river border is considered the most likely flashpoint in Bosnia and both sides have stepped up their rhetoric ahead of the arbitration.

Lawyers from both entities were expected to present evidence before a three-member arbitration panel, comprising chairman Roberts Owen, a U.S. lawyer, Cazim Sadikovic of the federation and Vitomir Popovic from the Serb republic.
The Moslem-Croat federation argues that Brcko should be awarded to the federation because Moslems and Croats formed a majority of the pre-war population.
They say allowing the Serbs to retain control of the town would reward "ethnic cleansing" and violence.

The Moslem chairman of the Bosnian presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, has predicted the federation will prevail in the arbitration but has also warned the Serbs that they no longer enjoy military superiority over the federation.
Separatist Serb forces backed by neighbouring Serbia expelled Moslems and Croats from the area after seizing the town early in the 1992-95 conflict.

Plavsic and other Bosnian Serb leaders accused Western powers of conspiring to split Serb territory in two and insisted that only the boundaries around Brcko were up for negotiation, not control of the town itself.
"A town which is a link between two halves of the Serb republic, our lifeline, cannot be an object of dispute," Plavsic said.
The NATO-led Stabilisation Force policing the peace treaty in Bosnia said it was following the arbitration closely and warned against provocative rhetoric.

"SFOR feels that any verbal posturing that goes on between the two parties is very unhelpful and doesn't contribute towards a decent solution," spokesman Major Andrew Saddleton told reporters in Sarajevo.
